extracted.intended_audience: novice and practicing mathematicians (graduate students, researchers, authors) who write research papers, expository articles, books, letters, referee reports, grant proposals, and talks
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for composing clear, precise, and effective mathematical writing across formats (research papers, expository articles, abstracts, books, letters, referee reports, talks, CVs, grant proposals). Emphasizes audience-awareness, organization, precision of language and notation, and multiple stages of revision and proofreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something to say
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to write effectively and well, you must have something to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin writing until you have an idea worth recording; the single most important fact about writing is having content. Start writing when you have something to say and know clearly why you are saying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have an audience, and you must know consciously who that audience is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you are writing for yourself, Mom, students, referees, or fellow specialists and write for that person/group. Picture a specific real person in your acquaintance as the intended reader to anticipate questions and confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for the reader (not to convince yourself)
rubrics_metrics.description: As you write you must think of your reader—not yourself; consider the reader’s convenience and understanding rather than your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing as if the text is only a record for yourself; state definitions, theorems, and structure explicitly so readers can follow. Don’t hide behind details or omit formal statements because the author already understands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say what you mean; mean what you say
rubrics_metrics.description: Use language so that your subject, referents, modifiers, and clauses actually convey the intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dangling participles and misplaced modifiers (examples given: “As a valued customer of XYZ Co., your call is very important to us.”). Recast sentences so modifiers clearly attach to their intended subject; read sentences aloud and check whether they would be understood in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of word choice and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words carefully and precisely; consult a dictionary when unsure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t misuse words (examples: 'enervate' ≠ 'invigorate'). Avoid sloppiness in ordinary prose; respect mathematical precision (do not use 'continuous' to mean 'measurable'). Choose memorable, appropriate names and notation (good names like 'continuous' are worth careful selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear ordering vs. nonlinear thought — manage digressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Written discourse is linearly ordered while thought is often nonlinear; learn to handle digressions, asides, parentheses, and footnotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when you digress and use parentheses, brackets, or clear markers. Train yourself to wrestle with linear presentation of ideas so the reader can follow the chain of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to start and when to stop writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Start writing when you have something to say and know your audience; stop when you have said what you have to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say it clearly, completely, forcefully, without lacunae, but avoid needless prattle. Concision and finality are virtues once the point is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh the effect of language — language as a weapon
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that words have power and can influence readers’ perceptions and social attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phrasing carefully (examples: 'self-styled radical leader' downgrades someone). When influential, your words carry responsibility; consider the broader impact of terms and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing clarifies thought — use writing as a tool for thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to think clearly and to write clearly are inextricably linked; writing can develop and hone ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short essays, drafts, and written explanations to identify logical gaps, separate hypotheses from assumptions, and order arguments. Writing up ideas forces you to treat 'obvious lemmas' and edge cases that you may have mentally glossed over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud for sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading your work aloud helps detect problems of sense and sound and develops an 'ear' for good prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many good writers read drafts aloud (examples: Laurence Olivier rehearsing). Reading aloud highlights awkward phrasing, repetitious sounds, and titles/terminology that lack resonance; it improves choice of words and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading via multiple focused passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofreading is essential and should be done in multiple passes, each with a specific focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended passes: (1) spelling and simple syntax (software can help), (2) accuracy, (3) organization and logic, (4) sense and flow of ideas, (5) sound, (6) overall coherence. Paul Halmos read every word six times—use multiple readings with distinct goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of notation and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notation and terminology carefully; they organize thought and affect perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, conventional, and memorable terms (e.g., 'continuous' rather than 'non-hypererratic'). Avoid overusing classification numbers or cryptic notation; define notation explicitly and place definitions conspicuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the paper clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical paper should have clear organization: introduction, definitions, theorems, proofs, bibliography, and front/back matter as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an outline and table of contents to plan structure; make stopping/entry points for readers clear; place definitions where they are needed; state theorems succinctly and give context in the introduction. (See TOC and section headings such as 'How to Organize a Paper', 'How to State a Theorem', 'How to Prove a Theorem'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State theorems and definitions precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: State theorems in clear, direct sentences and give precise definitions; limit definitions to those necessary and place them logically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague phrasing. Provide the statement of a theorem (preferably in one sentence), indicate hypotheses and conclusions exactly, and use 'if and only if' where appropriate. The book contains dedicated sections on 'How to State a Theorem' and 'How to State a Definition'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize proofs for reader comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should be organized, with the chain of reasoning made explicit and 'obvious' lemmas treated when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not defer or omit cases you mentally swept aside. Use structure within proofs (outline, lemmas, clear transitions), and make reasoning accessible rather than terse notes to yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples, context, and historical placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Place results in context by giving examples, history, and motivation so readers understand significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast bald statements with contextual paragraphs that explain who worked on the problem, why it mattered, and what followed. A simple claim ('The conjecture of Gauss (1830) is false.') should be expanded with background when appropriate to aid comprehension and appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary jargon and excessive specialization in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume all readers share the same background; avoid writing as if everyone is a top expert in your subfield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor level and notation to your intended audience; define specialized terms when first used and avoid 'notation is as in my last paper' style. For textbooks and expository work, write for students rather than instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear sentence structure and check grammar/syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure subject-verb agreement, correct pronoun references, avoid dangling modifiers, and use appropriate constructions rather than clumsy or ambiguous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and lists of errors (dangling participles, misplaced modifiers) illustrate pitfalls. Check for run-on sentences, split infinitives only when necessary, and maintain clarity rather than pedantic strictness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose titles, names, and terminology with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles, terms, and notation affect perception and memorability; choose them to convey meaning and to be memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good title or name (e.g., 'For Whom the Bell Tolls' vs. a bland variant) evokes imagery and helps reception; spend time picking good terminology and notation to aid future readers and adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology and tools judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage computers, TEX/LaTeX, spell-checkers and grammar checkers, but beware of overreliance and portability issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use software to help with spelling and basic syntax (Section 6.4 referenced). Keep backups, manage files carefully, and preview typeset output. Be aware of limitations of word processors vs. TeX for mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and professional in evaluative documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing letters of recommendation, referee reports, or grant self-evaluations, be specific, truthful, and professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete evidence and specificity rather than vague puffery; avoid inflation and damning-with-faint-praise; follow etiquette for declining to write recommendations when appropriate. (See sections 'The Letter of Recommendation' and 'The Referee’s Report'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan revision and publication strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about where to submit, how to revise based on referee reports, and what to do with the paper once written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select journals thoughtfully (consider audience and ranking), prepare cover letters and follow Instructions for Submission, handle referee reports respectfully and constructively, and consider preprint servers and electronic dissemination (sections on 'Where to Submit', 'Preprint Servers', 'MathSciNet').
